notes.1: This proved to be an exceptionally well answered opening question. Almost all of the candidates were able to find the two “critical values” of 4 . 5 and − 0 . 5 . The majority were able to go on and earn the final mark by identifying the two required regions correctly, but some were unable to do this. It is not easy to decide exactly how to express the statement when it is in the form of this case but, while the contradictory statement − 0 . 5 > x > 4 . 5 was not accepted, any reasonable combination of the two regions connected with and/or was accepted. Some candidates, impressively, used set notation writing their answer as { x : x < − 0 . 5 } ∪ { x : x > 4 . 5 } . Answers : x < − 0 . 5 , x > 4 . 5

notes.8: Many candidates produced completely correct answers to parts (i) and (ii) . There were some who were obviously aware of the formulae for an arc length and the area of a sector but did not reach the required explicit equation. Part (iii) proved more difficult and there were a handful of candidates who did not reject x = 6 , y = − 2 , which satisfied the equations but not the practical situation that the equations represented. 2 2 Answers : (i ) y = 3 x − 20 (ii) y = x − 32 (iii) x = 9 , y = 7 0606 Additional Mathematics November 2012
notes.9: The majority of candidates were able to answer both part (a)(i) and part (b)(i) correctly. Part (a)(ii) was less well done with a significant number giving an answer of 5 ! × 4 ! but omitting × 3 ! ; a smaller number gave the answer as 3!. Part (b)(ii) proved to be beyond virtually all candidates; perhaps the most straightforward way to reach the required answer was to find the number of ways which included both cousins and then to subtract this number from the answer to part (b)(i) . Answers : (a)(i) 3628800 (ii) 17280 (b)(i) 150 (ii) 110
notes.10: This was another question which was well done but it also proved to be a good discriminator. Most of the strong candidates scored full marks while the weakest were, usually, able to score some marks for knowing how to apply the remainder theorem. There were a number who found f(2) and f(1) and equated both of these to zero. This did lead to the correct value for c but led to an incorrect value of b . Where candidates tried to use this value of b it sometimes led to a problem in part (ii) . Some candidates correctly expressed the given polynomial as ( x − 8 ) ( x + x + 3 ) and just stated that x = 8 was the only root, without investigating the possibility of irrational roots.
notes.11: The two parts of this question were equally popular. OR proved to be a better source of marks than EITHER. In both options the majority of candidates did not appreciate the significance of the twelfth/third second. Instead they found the distance travelled in the first twelve/three seconds. This is the last session where there will be an option in the final question. Either In part (i) the majority of candidates did not appreciate the significance of the twelfth second. Instead they merely substituted t = 12 and gave 49.6 as the answer. The stronger candidates who realised the need to equate the differential of the given expression to zero were usually successful in part (ii) . Again most of those who appreciated the need for calculus were able to reach the correct answer. Answers : (i) 13.8 (ii) 4 (iii) 1.9 About half of the candidates who chose this option scored seven marks: one in part (i) , two in part (ii) and four in part (iii) . In part (ii) the majority of candidates did not appreciate the significance of the third second. Instead they found the distance travelled in the first three seconds. In part (iii) few were awarded the final mark, as the majority found the value of t which gave the minimum velocity but did not proceed to find this velocity.
